title: Local- and regional-scale air pollution modelling (PM(10)) and exposure assessment for pregnancy trimesters, infancy, and childhood to age 15 years: Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents And Children (ALSPAC).
ehr_evidence: The study used residential address history from the ALSPAC contact database and hourly PM10 measurements from the UK Automatic Urban and Rural Network (AURN) monitoring sites.
summary: Development and evaluation of local and regional-scale PM10 dispersion models to estimate individual-level historical air pollution exposures from pregnancy through age 15 years for the ALSPAC birth cohort.
key_findings: PM10 exposures declined on average by 11.6 μg/m3 from the first year of life (mean 31.2 μg/m3) to age ~15 (mean 19.6 μg/m3).
Intra-subject exposure contrasts were largest between pregnancy trimesters (5th to 95th centile: 24.4–37.3 μg/m3).
Local sources contributed 18.5%–19.5% during pregnancy/infancy and 14.4%–17.0% for longer periods, with main roads contributing ~3.0%.
Model evaluation showed good correlation with measured weekly PM10 concentrations (r = 0.71, p < 0.001), though the model underestimated concentrations (MB = -4.1 μg/m3, MPB = 21%).
study_design: Methodological exposure assessment study using dispersion modelling within a prospective birth cohort
data_source_type: Birth cohort (ALSPAC) with environmental monitoring and dispersion modelling data
population: Children in the ALSPAC birth cohort from pregnancy through age ~15 years, residing in the Avon region/south west England
exposure_domain: Air pollution (PM10), including local (traffic, industry, housing) and regional/long-range sources
limitations: Single monitoring site used for model evaluation
Lack of historic emissions data for specific industrial and domestic sources
Inability to model terrain, buildings, and wet deposition effects
Use of constant value for natural PM10 sources due to lack of pre-1993 monitoring data
Potential overestimation of background concentrations from imputed central site data
